title: Python Comments
learningObjectives: Explain why comments are used in source code.
Write single-line comments with the hash character.
Use comments to clarify intent without restating obvious code.
Recognize that ordinary triple-quoted strings are not a dedicated block-comment syntax.
Keep comments accurate as code changes.

understand.concept: Comments are explanatory text in source code that Python ignores during normal execution. A hash character (#) begins a comment that continues to the end of the physical line, unless it occurs inside a string literal. Python has no dedicated block-comment delimiter. Several consecutive # comment lines are the conventional way to write a multi-line comment. Triple-quoted strings are string literals and are commonly used for docstrings in specific documentation positions; they should not be described as block comments.
understand.whyItMatters: Useful comments preserve design intent, explain non-obvious decisions and help maintainers understand constraints. Unnecessary or outdated comments create noise and can mislead readers.
understand.analogy: A comment is like a margin note in a recipe: it explains why a step matters without becoming an ingredient or instruction executed by the kitchen.
understand.analogyLimit: Unlike a margin note, a Python comment is part of the source text and is discarded by the parser; it does not appear in a program's runtime output.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Single-line comments

A `#` outside a string literal begins a comment. Python ignores the comment text through the end of that physical line. A comment can occupy a line by itself or follow a statement.

## 2. Multi-line explanations

Python does not define a special block-comment token. For a multi-line explanation, write several consecutive lines beginning with `#`. This keeps the text clearly marked as comments.

## 3. Comments and strings are different

A hash character inside a quoted string is ordinary string content. Triple-quoted strings create string objects; they are not comments merely because they span multiple lines. A docstring is a string literal placed in a module, class or function body as its first statement and is available through documentation attributes.

## 4. Write useful comments

Explain why a non-obvious choice was made, document a constraint or clarify a surprising algorithm. Prefer clear names and simple code over comments that repeat each line. Update or remove comments when behaviour changes.

examples.title: A full-line comment
examples.code:
# Calculate the final number of seats
seats_per_row = 8
rows = 4
print(seats_per_row * rows)
examples.explanation: The comment explains the purpose of the calculation and is not executed.

examples.title: An end-of-line comment
examples.code:
tax_rate = 0.05  # Example rate for this exercise
price = 200
print(price * tax_rate)
examples.explanation: The hash begins a comment after the assignment. The rate is data and the comment does not change it.

examples.title: Several comment lines
examples.code:
# Step 1: collect the values
# Step 2: calculate the total
values = [3, 4, 5]
print(sum(values))
examples.explanation: Consecutive hash-prefixed lines provide a multi-line explanation without a special block-comment syntax.

examples.title: A hash inside a string
examples.code:
message = 'Use # to start a comment in source code'
print(message)
examples.expectedOutput: Use # to start a comment in source code
examples.explanation: The hash is inside a quoted string, so it is part of the value rather than the start of a comment.

examples.title: A function docstring
examples.code:
def area(width, height):
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return width * height

print(area(6, 4))
examples.explanation: The triple-quoted first statement is a docstring associated with the function. It is a string object used for documentation, not a general block comment.

practise.guidedTask: Add one comment above a calculation explaining the business rule it implements. Then remove any comment that simply repeats an obvious variable assignment.
practise.independentTask: Write a small program that calculates the total cost of two items. Add concise comments explaining the purpose of the inputs and any non-obvious calculation. Include a string containing a # character.
hints: A hash outside a string begins a comment.
A comment ends at the end of its physical line.
Use multiple # lines for a multi-line explanation.
A hash inside quotes is ordinary string data.
Use a docstring to document a module, class or function; do not call every triple-quoted string a comment.
practise.challenge: Review a short program and replace redundant comments with meaningful names. Add one comment explaining a genuine design decision and one docstring for a public function.

questions.prompt: Which character begins a Python comment outside a string?
questions.explanation: The hash character begins a comment through the end of the physical line.

questions.prompt: What happens to a normal source-code comment during program execution?
options: It is ignored by the Python parser/runtime
questions.answer: It is ignored by the Python parser/runtime
questions.explanation: Comments are not executable statements and do not produce runtime output.

questions.prompt: How is a conventional multi-line comment written in Python?
questions.explanation: Python has no dedicated block-comment delimiter; repeated hash-prefixed lines are conventional.

questions.prompt: Is the # character inside a quoted string a comment marker?
options: Yes, it always ends the string
questions.explanation: Comment syntax is recognized outside string literals; inside a string, # is ordinary data.

options: A string literal used to document a module, class or function
questions.answer: A string literal used to document a module, class or function
questions.explanation: A docstring is a string literal placed as the first statement in a module, class or function body.
